anomaly_def.Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer persistently chooses sub-optimal execution plans despite reasonably accurate statistics, leading to excessive I/O, row visits, or parallelism misuse.
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Obsolete row versions and rollback records accumulate faster than background cleanup can reclaim them, inflating tables/indexes and adding visibility-check overhead.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database back-end and maintenance processes drive host CPU utilization to saturation, creating run-queue waits and pervasive latency spikes.

When all three conditions coexist, the database exhibits a blended failure pattern: queries flip to or remain on inefficient plans that scan or join far more rows than necessary; the scanned pages are bloated with dead tuples, so every logical row access requires extra visibility checks and additional buffer churn; the surplus work manifests as sustained CPU saturation, causing system-wide slowdowns. Autovacuum or garbage-collection workers run constantly yet make little progress because they compete for the same exhausted CPU, while critical user queries also stall on CPU run-queue waits. Statistics drift as table bloat grows, amplifying plan instability and fostering new mis-plans. Symptoms include erratic plan changes, explosive growth of table and index size, skyrocketing CPU wait events, and workload latency that degrades non-linearly with concurrency.

Causally, poor plan choices initiate oversized scans and high row lookups, inflating CPU consumption and prolonging transaction lifetimes; the longer execution times delay cleanup horizon advancement, letting MVCC garbage pile up. The ensuing table bloat further skews cardinality estimates, nudging the optimizer toward even worse plans—especially when plan reuse locks in bad strategies—creating a vicious feedback loop. Meanwhile, the compounded read-amplification from dead rows and the CPU-intensive mis-plans jointly saturate the processor, throttling both foreground queries and background vacuuming. The throttled cleanup then falls further behind, intensifying version accumulation and perpetuating the cycle until the system experiences severe throughput collapse or reaches transaction-ID wraparound danger.

entry.official_definition: Specifies the number of TCP keepalive messages that can be lost before the server connection to the client is considered dead.
entry.trigger_condition: The number of lost TCP keepalive probes reaches tcp_keepalives_count on systems supporting TCP_KEEPCNT.
entry.workload_impact: The server can consider the client connection dead after the configured keepalive failure threshold.
entry.default_behavior: Default value is 0, selecting the operating system default.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when connection establishment, authentication exchange, or session activity does not progress within the allowed time budget.
entry.solution_guidance: Check connection lifecycle, client responsiveness, authentication latency, idle-session handling, and whether connection pools are holding stale sessions.
